items.title: Headlines for November 10, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## GOP Rep. Thomas Massie Introduces Articles of Impeachment Against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth Nov 10, 2026 Republican Congressmember Thomas Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Monday for “high crimes and misdemeanors.” The eight impeachment articles accuse Hegseth of violating the 1973 War Powers Resolution by continuing to attack Iran even after both chambers of Congress ordered the Trump administration to stop. He’s also accused of illegally waging war against Yemen, ignoring laws designed to reduce civilian casualties, overseeing “extrajudicial killings” in attacks on boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific, abducting Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro without congressional authorization, and suppressing the free speech rights of Democratic Senator Mark Kelly in retaliation for reminding troops not to obey illegal orders. Congressmember Massie outlined the charges during a speech from the House floor. > Rep. Thomas Massie: “Wherefore, Secretary of Defense Peter Hegseth, by such conduct, has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law, Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust or profit under the United States.” It’s expected the House will vote on Hegseth’s impeachment on Wednesday. Only a few Republican defectors would be needed for a simple majority, setting up a Senate trial on whether to remove Hegseth. On Monday, President Trump said he would stand by Hegseth if he’s impeached. ## Pentagon Retreats from Second U.K. Base Due to Alleged Threat from Iran Nov 10, 2026 The Wall Street Journal reports the Pentagon has evacuated aircraft from a second base in the United Kingdom due to another alleged threat from Iran. U.S. refueling tankers were reportedly moved from a base in Mildenhall on Monday. Last month, the Pentagon pulled B-1 bombers out of another British base. Meanwhile, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says two more ships, including a supertanker, are on fire near the Strait of Hormuz after using what Iranian officials have called an “unauthorized route.” Iran has claimed 11 strikes on ships over a 10-day span. The continued attacks on shipping came as Iran’s Foreign Ministry said it could reopen the strait within 48 hours if the U.S. agrees to Tehran’s list of demands. > Esmail Baghaei: “If the U.S. meets the demands put forward by Iran, the situation in the region could see a positive shift in as little as two days, and security in the Strait of Hormuz could also be restored.” On Monday, President Trump spoke with Qatar’s prime minister, who’s acted as a mediator in efforts to end the war. After the talks, Trump claimed there was “positive momentum” in negotiations for a deal with Iran. > President Donald Trump: “The military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing, but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes. Israel and the entire Middle East are protected from Iranian danger and threats, and we’re seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it’s going to be ending fairly soon.” Since the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Iran in February, Trump has claimed more than 40 times that the war was close to an end, that a deal was near, or that the war was already over.

items.title: Early Edition: November 10, 2026
items.excerpt: IRAN WAR President Trump yesterday reiterated that a renewed military campaign against Iran is “quite unlikely,” and “doesn’t seem to be necessary.” Trump’s comments were made on social media and at an impromptu press conference, and he added that “we want a long-term solution.” Trump told Reuters that Qatar and Saudi Arabia were eager for a peaceful solution to the Iran conflict but that the United States was ready to resume military strikes if necessary. Barak Ravid reports for Axios; Steve Holland reports for Reuters. Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani on social media yesterday described his talks with Trump and U.S. Vice President JD Vance about Iran as “positive.” The prime minister said he was “grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region.” France’s foreign minister today said the Qatari prime minister will make an unscheduled stop at the G7 foreign ministers meeting in Paris, France. Tara Suter reports for The Hill; John Irish reports for Reuters. IRAN WAR – OTHER DEVELOPMENTS France yesterday accused Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of being behind last month’s temperature-raising hack of French supermarket fridges and freezers. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the attack was “unprecedented in both its scale and its level of aggression,” and added that those responsible would be hit with sanctions. Iranian media outlets have dismissed the allegations as baseless, while France today summoned Iran’s ambassador. Ella Kipling and Joe Tidy report for BBC News; John Irish reports for Reuters. Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand at the G7 meeting today said Canada reimposed sanctions on 11 Iranian entities for their contribution to Iran’s nuclear activities and ballistic missile program. Anand said the measures were intended to restrict Iran’s access to funding and sensitive technology linked to its nuclear and missile programs. Rishabh Jaiswal reports for Reuters. The United States yesterday evacuated U.S. aircraft from the U.K. Royal Air Force base in Mildenhall in the wake of a threat from Iran, sources told the Wall Street Journal. The sources said the precise nature of the threat to RAF Mildenhall remains under discussion among U.S. officials. Shelby Holliday and Alexander Ward report. RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR Russian and Ukrainian officials today met in Abu Dhabi for their first U.S.-brokered talks since Feb. 2026. U.S. Special Envoy Jared Kushner told delegates that recent contacts with both sides had “really identified, narrowed the gaps,” and that Trump was committed to achieving peace. Roula Rouhana reports for Reuters. The White House is “cautiously optimistic” about the peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi this week, U.S. officials told Axios. A U.S. official said the “relations we have built with [Russian President Vladimir] Putin will be instrumental in these negotiations,” while another U.S. official said U.S. Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner may travel to Ukraine and Russia to speak directly with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Putin. Barak Ravid reports. Russia believes the main thrust of U.S.-brokered peace talks on Ukraine should be seeking agreement on the main elements of a post-war security framework for Europe, a source in the Russian delegation told Reuters. The source said the Ukrainian settlement “is just one aspect of this wide-ranging discussion and is subordinate to the main objective – the creation of a comprehensive and indivisible security architecture for the entire continent.” Andrew Osborn reports.

items.title: CPI inflation report: October 2026
items.excerpt: Costs for goods and services rose more than expected in October, providing fresh warning signs for the Federal Reserve in its fight to lower inflation. The consumer price index, a broad gauge of costs across the U.S. economy, increased a seasonally adjusted 0.4% for the month, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for a 0.3% increase. Stripping out volatile food and energy, so-called core CPI increased 0.3% against the forecast for a 0.2% gain. The headline CPI had increased 0.6% in September while core was up 0.3%. The report comes at a critical juncture for the Federal Reserve as it considers its next interest-rate move. Speaking Tuesday morning in London ahead of the CPI release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for a half-point increase in December, and specifically said such a hike should be on the table if core CPI was "around 0.3." Hours later, that's exactly what happened. Traders are now fully pricing in a quarter percentage-point increase when the Fed next meets Dec. 8-9, and put odds of a half-point hike at 13.6%, after being around zero prior to the inflation report, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Stocks fell following the release, while Treasury yields jumped. "This was the report the market could least afford to see," said Karen Manna, fixed income investment strategist at Federated Hermes. "A hotter inflation print raises fresh questions about whether the Fed has done enough to contain price pressures and reinforces the risk that interest rates need to move higher and stay there for longer." The BLS did not estimate a yearly rate in its October inflation report. The government shutdown last year prevented the bureau from collecting sufficient data in October 2025, so there is no comparable figure to use. However, the report did include annual figures for some individual items where it was able to collect data. Though gasoline prices have been falling in recent weeks, the energy index rose 0.7% and the gasoline index was up 1%. The natural gas index, though, was off 0.8%. Food costs accelerated 0.5%, pushed higher by increases of 1% for snacks, 0.9% for beef and 0.5% for meats, poultry, fish and eggs. Transportation services jumped 0.8%. New vehicle prices increased 0.2% but used cars and trucks fell 1.2%. Shelter costs were higher by 0.3%, which the BLS said accounted for more than 30% of the headline increase. Apparel, a tariff-sensitive sector, rose just 0.1%. Medical care commodities prices increased 0.5%. Airline fares accelerated 0.4%. At the Fed's October meeting, central bank officials voted 10-2 to keep their benchmark rate in a range between 3.75%-4% while awaiting incoming data. ... Despite the moderating gas prices recently, Fed officials have expressed concern that the impacts from the Iran war and President Donald Trump's tariffs are becoming embedded in the economy. Inflation has been running above the Fed's 2% target for some 5½ years. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, speaking Tuesday after the inflation report, said she sees a need for two additional quarter-point increases. Logan noted that the CPI report was "higher than expected" and said she is worried that the Fed's primary inflation-forecasting metric, the personal consumption expenditures price index, also could move higher when it is reported later in November. "It may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the [Federal Open Market Committee] has moved so far this fall," she said. "After two more increases are in place, it would make sense in my view to pause and examine economic and financial developments to determine what further action may be appropriate." In addition to tariffs and the war, inflation has been pressured by hyperscaler spending in the artificial intelligence buildout. Electricity prices rose 0.9%, a potential complication from the AI story. Consumers, though, continue to spend — retail sales rose 0.8% in September, according to the Commerce Department — and businesses are still raising prices. A net 37% of businesses responding to the October National Federation of Independent Business survey reported that they plan to raise prices in the next three months, the highest level since July 2022.

items.title: Gas prices dip below $4 but inflation remains stubbornly high
items.excerpt: The average price of gasoline dipped below $4 a gallon Tuesday for the first time in three months, according to AAA. The price of regular gas has fallen by 38 cents in the last month to a national average of $3.98. The overall cost of living, however, remains stubbornly high. Consumer prices in October were up 0.4% from the previous month, according to a report Tuesday from the Labor Department. That's a bigger monthly increase than forecasters had expected. Rising housing costs accounted for about a third of the monthly increase. Grocery prices were also up sharply during the month. ... The drop in gasoline prices in recent weeks is thanks to a combination of falling crude oil prices, refineries' switch to a cheaper blend of winter fuel, and the typical seasonal drop in demand for gas.

items.excerpt: "Core inflation today reflects three outsized shocks: tariffs, energy prices, and AI-related demand," Josh Hirt, senior U.S. economist at Vanguard Group, an asset manager, wrote in an e-mail Tuesday. The Iran war has raised oil prices, pushing up prices for fuels like gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, which are refined from crude oil, economists said. Gasoline prices rose 1% in October, a significant pullback after a 9.1% monthly increase in September, CPI data showed. While diesel prices have retreated from recent record highs, they remain elevated and could spill more broadly into the U.S. economy in the coming months, economists said. "Diesel prices have a really slow pass-through to all the areas of CPI, given it affects transportation costs," said Thomas Ryan, a senior North America economist at Capital Economics. "These things take time," Ryan said. "It'll be an inflationary impetus for at least the next three to six months, I suspect." There was some evidence of that broader percolation of diesel prices in October, such as in food prices, Zandi said. Higher diesel prices add to the cost of transporting food to the grocery store shelves, he said.

Thomas Massie: “Wherefore, Secretary of Defense Peter Hegseth, by such conduct, has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law, Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust or profit under the United States.” It’s expected the House will vote on Hegseth’s impeachment on Wednesday. Only a few Republican defectors would be needed for a simple majority, setting up a Senate trial on whether to remove Hegseth. On Monday, President Trump said he would stand by Hegseth if he’s impeached. ... ## Trump Raises New Election Conspiracy Theory After Democrats Sweep Midterms Nov 10, 2026 Democrats are continuing to build on their historic wins in last week’s midterm elections as votes continue to be counted. In Mississippi, Scott Colom’s lead over Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith has topped 2,500 votes, with just two batches of ballots left to be counted before a Friday deadline to certify the results. In Colorado, Republican Congressmember Lauren Boebert is trailing in her bid to hold on to her seat. On Monday, CNN projected Boebert will lose the race to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired U.S. Navy admiral who served on the National Security Council under President Joe Biden. On Monday, President Trump reversed his previous comment that he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results of the midterm elections. Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, “Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???” ## Schumer Faces Pressure to Step Aside as Chris Van Hollen Hints at Run for Senate Majority Leader Senate Democrats could be headed for a leadership shakeup, after Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen indicated Monday he’s open to running for Senate majority leader when the new Congress convenes in January. A source close to Van Hollen told Politico the Maryland Democrat is thinking about a run after he “received an outpouring of calls and is now in active listening mode. The door is not shut.” This comes as a growing number of Senate Democrats have called for new leadership or refused to commit to supporting New York Senator Chuck Schumer for majority leader. Joining the call is a major labor union, the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, which wrote in a letter to Schumer on Monday, “We believe this is the right moment for a new generation to lead Senate Democrats.” Meanwhile, Connecticut Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal said he’s open to new leadership if a challenger to Schumer emerges. > Sen. Richard Blumenthal: “But we need to have a conversation about leadership going forward, because we need new energy and ideas.” ## Senate Advances Bill to Speed Construction of Fossil Fuel Projects and Data Centers In more news from Capitol Hill, the Senate voted 73 to 25 Monday to take up a sweeping permitting reform bill. It was advanced by nearly every Republican and 22 Democrats. Environmental groups have called the legislation an “aggressive attack on federal environmental protections in order to facilitate rapid, unregulated development of fracked gas power plants, dirty fossil fuel pipelines, and expensive hyperscale data centers.” Meanwhile, Indigenous leaders, including New Mexico Governor-elect Deb Haaland, argue the bill would undermine tribal sovereignty. More than 160 health, consumer, religious and environmental groups are calling on Congress to instead pass the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act. It’s sponsored by Michigan democratic socialist Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib, who said, “[The] elections send a clear message that Americans want their representatives to protect their health and environment, not sell them out to Big Tech and Big Oil.” ... ## SCOTUS Allows Trump Admin to Resume Border Wall Construction in Big Bend National Park The U.S. Supreme Court is allowing the Trump administration to resume the construction of a new border wall in Big Bend National Park and along more than 500 miles of the Rio Grande in Texas. Monday’s ruling lifted a lower court’s temporary injunction that blocked construction back in October while a lawsuit filed by the Center for Biological Diversity and others is resolved. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only Supreme Court member to dissent. Click here to see our coverage of this story.

items.title: Entertainment news roundup: 10 November 2026 | SVCZZ
items.excerpt: Godzilla Minus Zero has opened to a record $31.6 million for a live-action foreign-language film in North America. Ramayana: Rise of a Legend took Rs 107.50 crore in India on its fifth day, the biggest Monday ever for a Bollywood film, and Purna Bahadur Ko Sarangi has become the highest-grossing Nepali film ever. ## Box office Godzilla Minus Zero opened to $31.6 million in North America, a record debut for a live-action foreign-language film at the North American box office, according to Sunday studio estimates reported by the Associated Press. The film took about $17 million in Japan over the same weekend, and $21.3 million of its takings came from IMAX screens worldwide. The Associated Press notes the one exception among live-action films: 2004’s Passion of the Christ opened to $83.8 million. Takashi Yamazaki’s film is the sequel to Godzilla Minus One. Ramayana: Rise of a Legend earned Rs 107.50 crore net in India on day 5, Monday 9 November, its biggest single day so far and the biggest Monday ever for a Bollywood film, passing Dhurandhar 2 and its Rs 64 crore. The five-day India net stands at Rs 346.35 crore, with India gross at Rs 413.90 crore. All figures are Sacnilk estimates reported by Times Now, as of 10 November 2026. Rs 343.6 million in 17 days has made Purna Bahadur Ko Sarangi the highest-grossing Nepali film ever. Producer Binod Paudel shared the figure, which passes the previous record of Rs 235 million set by Kabaddi 4. The film also set a record single-day gross of Rs 38.9 million on 9 November 2026. Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine sits at 94 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 217 reviews, as of 10 November 2026. The espionage comedy stars John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell and is set on Easter Island shortly before the 1973 Chilean coup. It opened wide on 6 November 2026. On Rotten Tomatoes, Ramayana: Rise of a Legend holds 76 percent from 46 critic reviews, with a 90 percent verified audience score from more than 250 ratings, as of 7 November 2026. ScreenRant rated the film 7 out of 10. Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, the film stars Ranbir Kapoor, Sai Pallavi, Yash and Sunny Deol. ## Trailers and first looks The trailer for Gobar Ganesh has been released at a launch event in Kathmandu. The Nepali film is directed by Marichman Shrestha and stars Balchhi Dhurbe and Barsha Siwakoti. It is scheduled for release on Magh 1. The trailer for Melania, The Series is out, ahead of the two-part docuseries reaching Prime Video on 20 November 2026. It follows the documentary film released earlier this year. A trailer is out for Darius Rucker: They Called Me Hootie, the documentary that premieres on Hulu on 16 November 2026. It traces the singer’s path from his Hootie and the Blowfish years to country stardom. Briarcliff Entertainment has released the official trailer for Drag, a dark comedy thriller starring Lizzy Caplan and Lucy DeVito as burglar sisters trapped in a home invasion. The film arrives in US theatres on 29 January 2027. Raviv Ullman and Greg Yagolnitzer directed. MGM+ has released first-look images for Bosch: Start of Watch, with Cameron Monaghan as a 26-year-old Harry Bosch in 1992 Los Angeles alongside Omari Hardwick as veteran LAPD officer Eli Bridges. The eight-episode prequel premieres on 10 January 2027 with two episodes, then weekly to the finale on 21 February. ## Casting Daniel MacPherson has joined Priyanka Chopra Jonas and Russell Crowe in the science-fiction thriller Bluefly, playing Dugan, a Special Forces soldier. Directed by Nimrod Antal, the Congo-set film starts shooting shortly on Australia’s Gold Coast. Universal’s Snoop Dogg biopic Snoop has added Aaron Paul as music executive Jimmy Iovine, with Giovanni Ribisi joining as attorney David Kenner. Jonathan Daviss stars as Snoop, and the film opens in theatres on 6 August 2027. Halsey’s horror film Replacer has added Carrie-Anne Moss to its cast. Directed by Avan Jogia, the film has finished shooting in Montreal, Lilly Wachowski executive produces, and it has no distributor or release date yet. Halsey plays Proxy, a troubled DJ stranded in Montreal. Nina Dobrev, Jack Whitehall, Greg Kinnear and Andie MacDowell will star in Daryl Wein’s romantic comedy Honeymooners, a story about second chances and finding love where it is least expected. Filming begins in Italy in the first quarter of 2027. ... The film reaches theatres on 1 October 2027. ... Heart of the Beast arrives on digital platforms today, 10 November 2026, to rent and purchase on PVOD from 12 a.m. ET, as confirmed by Paramount Home Entertainment. The David Ayer film, starring Brad Pitt, opened in cinemas on 25 September 2026. It is Certified Fresh at 84 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 185 reviews, with a 94 percent audience score. Jessica Chastain’s supernatural horror film Other Mommy makes its digital debut today, 10 November 2026, with 4K UHD, Blu-ray and DVD following on 29 December 2026, Universal Pictures Home Entertainment has announced. ... Netflix has set 13 November 2026 for Ranabaali, streaming in Telugu, Hindi, Tamil, Kannada and Malayalam. Netflix India confirmed the date on 9 November 2026. ... Prime Video’s global charts have a new number one: The Mongoose is the most-watched movie worldwide days after its international streaming rollout.
